pack.description: Phrasal verbs and conversational idioms heard in campus conversations, useful for Listen and Choose a Response and for natural spoken answers.
pack.selection_note: Internal high-yield selection of phrasal verbs and idioms common in everyday campus speech; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: to find the answer to something or understand it by thinking
entries.example_academic: Engineers eventually figured out why the bridge vibrated in high winds.
entries.example_spoken: I can't figure out how to submit this form.

entries.definition: to give a piece of work to the person who asked for it
entries.example_academic: Participants who turned in incomplete questionnaires were excluded from the analysis.
entries.example_spoken: Did you turn in your essay yet?

entries.definition: to give something, such as homework or a form, to a person in authority
entries.example_academic: Candidates must hand in all notes before leaving the examination room.
entries.example_spoken: I handed in the wrong file by mistake.

entries.definition: to leave a course, school or competition before finishing it
entries.example_academic: Students from low-income families are more likely to drop out in the first year.
entries.example_spoken: He dropped out of college to start a company.

entries.definition: to reach the same level as others after being behind; or to do work that should have been done earlier
entries.example_academic: Wages in the region have not caught up with those of the capital.
entries.example_spoken: I need the weekend to catch up on reading.

entries.definition: to fail to keep the same speed or level as others
entries.example_academic: Countries that neglected education fell behind their neighbors.
entries.example_spoken: If you skip two classes, you'll fall behind fast.

entries.definition: to put your name on a list in order to take part in something
entries.example_academic: More than two thousand volunteers signed up for the trial.
entries.example_spoken: I signed up for the yoga class on Tuesdays.

entries.definition: to try to find out the facts about a problem or situation
entries.example_academic: A committee was appointed to look into the causes of the accident.
entries.example_spoken: I'll look into it and email you tomorrow.

entries.definition: to think of an idea, plan or answer
entries.example_academic: The team came up with a cheaper way of purifying the water.
entries.example_spoken: We need to come up with a topic by Friday.

entries.definition: to delay doing something until a later time
entries.example_academic: The government put off the reform until after the election.
entries.example_spoken: I keep putting off my dentist appointment.

entries.definition: to use all of something so that none is left
entries.translation_fr: manquer de, ne plus avoir de
entries.example_academic: The expedition ran out of supplies two weeks before reaching the coast.
entries.example_spoken: We ran out of time before the last question.

entries.definition: to have a friendly relationship with someone
entries.example_academic: Employees who get along with their supervisors report less stress.
entries.example_spoken: Do you get along with your new roommate?

entries.definition: to feel happy and excited about something that is going to happen
entries.example_academic: The delegates looked forward to a more open discussion on the second day.
entries.example_spoken: I'm really looking forward to the break.

entries.definition: to get information about something, or to learn a fact for the first time
entries.example_academic: The survey was designed to find out how residents use the park.
entries.example_spoken: I just found out that the exam was moved.

entries.definition: to stop trying to do something, or to stop doing something you did regularly
entries.example_academic: Many farmers gave up growing cotton when prices collapsed.
entries.example_spoken: Don't give up; you're almost done.

entries.definition: to tell someone a fact that they had not noticed or thought about
entries.example_academic: Critics pointed out that the sample included no rural schools.
entries.example_spoken: She pointed out two mistakes in my slides.

entries.definition: to arrange, organize or start something
entries.example_academic: The foundation set up a fund to support young researchers.
entries.example_spoken: Can you help me set up the projector?

entries.definition: to collect someone or something; or to learn something without formal study
entries.example_academic: Children pick up the sounds of a second language more easily than adults.
entries.example_spoken: I'll pick up the books from the library on my way.

entries.definition: to take someone or something to a place and leave them there; or to become less
entries.example_academic: Attendance drops off sharply after the first month of the program.
entries.example_spoken: Could you drop off my form at the office?

entries.definition: to arrive at a place, especially when expected
entries.example_academic: Only half of the registered voters showed up at the polls.
entries.example_spoken: He showed up twenty minutes late, as usual.

entries.definition: to find the answer to something by thinking; to develop in a good way; or to exercise
entries.translation_fr: résoudre ; bien se passer ; faire de l'exercice
entries.example_academic: Astronomers worked out the comet's orbit from three observations.
entries.example_spoken: Don't worry, everything will work out.

entries.definition: to check or study something carefully from beginning to end
entries.example_academic: The editors went over the manuscript line by line.
entries.example_spoken: Let's go over the answers before we hand it in.

entries.definition: to refuse an offer or request; or to make sound or heat lower
entries.example_academic: The council turned down the application to build on the wetland.
entries.example_spoken: She turned down the job because it was too far away.

entries.definition: to start talking about a subject
entries.example_academic: Several members brought up the question of cost at the meeting.
entries.example_spoken: Don't bring up the deadline; he's already stressed.

entries.definition: to decide that a planned event will not happen
entries.example_academic: The organizers called off the conference because of the storm.
entries.example_spoken: They called off the game because of the rain.

entries.definition: to move or progress at the same speed as someone or something
entries.translation_fr: suivre le rythme de, se tenir au courant de
entries.example_academic: Supply could not keep up with the growth in demand.
entries.example_spoken: I can't keep up with all the reading for this class.

entries.definition: to do something that corrects or balances a bad situation
entries.example_academic: Higher exports made up for the fall in domestic sales.
entries.example_spoken: I'll work on Sunday to make up for missing Friday.

entries.definition: to borrow a book from a library; to look at something that seems interesting; or to pay and leave
entries.translation_fr: emprunter ; jeter un œil à ; régler et partir
entries.example_academic: Readers may check out up to ten items at a time.
entries.example_spoken: You should check out the new café on Main Street.

entries.definition: to write the necessary information on a form
entries.example_academic: Applicants must fill out a separate form for each grant.
entries.example_spoken: I had to fill out three forms to change my address.

entries.definition: to spend time relaxing, often with friends
entries.example_academic: Teenagers in the study preferred to hang out in public spaces rather than at home.
entries.example_spoken: We usually hang out at the student center after class.

entries.definition: to take action in order to solve a problem; or to be about a subject
entries.example_academic: The second chapter deals with the origins of the conflict.
entries.example_spoken: I'll deal with the booking if you send the emails.

entries.definition: to do a task, plan or study
entries.example_academic: The survey was carried out over a period of six months.
entries.example_spoken: We carried out the experiment twice to be sure.

entries.definition: to experience a difficult period; or to look at something carefully from start to finish
entries.example_academic: The industry went through a period of rapid consolidation.
entries.example_spoken: Let's go through the checklist one more time.

entries.definition: to accept a job or responsibility; or to begin to have a quality
entries.translation_fr: accepter, se charger de ; prendre (un aspect)
entries.example_academic: The state took on responsibilities once left to the church.
entries.example_spoken: I can't take on another project this month.

entries.definition: to reduce the amount of something that you use or spend
entries.example_academic: Households cut back on meat when prices rose.
entries.example_spoken: I'm trying to cut back on coffee.

entries.definition: to finally be in a place or situation that was not planned
entries.example_academic: Much of the plastic ends up in the ocean.
entries.example_spoken: We ended up studying until two in the morning.

entries.definition: to find or meet something or someone by chance; or to give a particular impression
entries.example_academic: Researchers came across the letters while cataloguing another collection.
entries.example_spoken: I came across a great article for our project.

entries.definition: to meet someone by chance; or to begin to experience a difficulty
entries.example_academic: The project ran into difficulties when funding was cut.
entries.example_spoken: I ran into our old professor at the supermarket.

entries.definition: to trust someone to do something, or to expect something to happen
entries.example_academic: Farmers could no longer count on regular rainfall.
entries.example_spoken: You can count on me to bring the slides.

entries.definition: to recover from an illness, a shock or a disappointment
entries.example_academic: The economy took almost a decade to get over the crisis.
entries.example_spoken: It took me a week to get over that cold.

entries.definition: something that is very easy to do
entries.example_academic: For experienced translators, the first passage was a piece of cake.
entries.example_spoken: The quiz was a piece of cake; I finished in ten minutes.

entries.definition: feeling slightly ill
entries.example_academic: Several players were under the weather, which may explain the team's poor result.
entries.example_spoken: I'm feeling a bit under the weather, so I'll stay home.

entries.definition: having the same understanding of a situation or plan
entries.example_academic: The two agencies were not on the same page about who should lead the response.
entries.example_spoken: Let's meet quickly so we're all on the same page.

entries.definition: to decide to stop working on something for now
entries.example_academic: After twelve hours of negotiation, the delegates called it a day.
entries.example_spoken: We've done enough; let's call it a day.

entries.definition: to watch someone or something carefully to make sure they are safe or to notice changes
entries.example_academic: Economists keep an eye on inventory levels for early signs of a slowdown.
entries.example_spoken: Can you keep an eye on my laptop for a minute?

entries.definition: to quickly improve a skill or your knowledge of something you learned before
entries.example_academic: New staff were asked to brush up on safety procedures before the inspection.
entries.example_spoken: I need to brush up on my statistics before the course starts.

entries.definition: to finally do something that you have intended to do for a long time
entries.translation_fr: trouver le temps de, finir par
entries.example_academic: The council never got around to repairing the oldest bridges.
entries.example_spoken: I still haven't got around to answering her email.

entries.definition: to reduce the number of possibilities or choices
entries.example_academic: Genetic testing narrowed down the possible causes to two.
entries.example_spoken: I've narrowed it down to two topics for my paper.

entries.definition: to start to suffer from an illness
entries.example_academic: Nearly a third of the crew came down with fever during the voyage.
entries.example_spoken: I think I'm coming down with the flu.

entries.definition: to fail to happen or to be completed, though it was planned
entries.example_academic: The merger fell through when regulators raised objections.
entries.example_spoken: Our trip fell through because nobody booked the tickets.

entries.definition: to solve small problems or disagreements before something can go ahead
entries.example_academic: The two sides met to iron out the remaining differences in the text.
entries.example_spoken: We still have a few details to iron out before the presentation.

entries.definition: to leave very little time to do something or arrive somewhere
entries.example_academic: The team cut it close, submitting the proposal minutes before the deadline.
entries.example_spoken: Leaving at eight is cutting it close; the exam starts at half past.

entries.definition: not yet decided or certain
entries.example_academic: The future of the program remained up in the air after the budget cuts.
entries.example_spoken: My summer plans are still up in the air.

entries.definition: to stay awake all night in order to study or finish work
entries.example_academic: Students who pull an all-nighter before an exam tend to recall less the next day.
entries.example_spoken: I pulled an all-nighter to finish the lab report.

entries.definition: unable to decide between two choices or opinions
entries.example_academic: Many voters were still on the fence a week before the election.
entries.example_spoken: I'm on the fence about taking that course.

entries.definition: to be the explanation for something; or to form a particular part of a total
entries.example_academic: Exports account for nearly half of the country's income.
entries.example_spoken: How do you account for the difference between the two results?

entries.definition: to decide that something is not possible or not suitable
entries.example_academic: The tests ruled out infection as the cause of the symptoms.
entries.example_spoken: We can rule out Friday; half the group is away.

entries.definition: to stop using or providing something gradually, in stages
entries.example_academic: The government plans to phase out coal power within fifteen years.
entries.example_spoken: They're phasing out paper forms next semester.

entries.definition: to have as its main or basic point
entries.example_academic: The dispute boils down to a disagreement over who owns the data.
entries.example_spoken: It all boils down to how much time we have.

entries.definition: to be as good as what was expected or promised
entries.example_academic: The new treatment failed to live up to the claims made for it.
entries.example_spoken: The movie didn't live up to the reviews.

entries.definition: to accept an unpleasant situation or person without complaining
entries.example_academic: Residents put up with the noise for months before complaining.
entries.example_spoken: I can't put up with that buzzing light anymore.

entries.definition: to have to deal with a difficulty or opposition
entries.example_academic: Reformers came up against strong resistance from landowners.
entries.example_spoken: We came up against a problem with the software.

entries.definition: to keep something, especially money or time, for a particular purpose; or to decide not to consider something for now
entries.example_academic: A portion of the budget was set aside for emergency repairs.
entries.example_spoken: Try to set aside an hour a day for reading.

entries.definition: to choose not to take part in something
entries.translation_fr: choisir de ne pas participer à, se retirer de
entries.example_academic: Employees may opt out of the pension plan at any time.
entries.example_spoken: Can I opt out of the group project and write an essay instead?

entries.definition: to include a particular fact or amount when you calculate or plan something
entries.example_academic: The estimate does not factor in the cost of training new staff.
entries.example_spoken: Did you factor in the time it takes to get there?

entries.definition: to direct all your attention toward one thing
entries.example_academic: Investigators zeroed in on a fault in the cooling system.
entries.example_spoken: Let's zero in on the two questions everyone got wrong.

entries.definition: to choose one person or thing from a group for special attention, praise or criticism
entries.example_academic: The report singles out transport as the fastest-growing source of emissions.
entries.example_spoken: The professor singled out her essay as the best in the class.

entries.definition: a small, visible part of a much larger problem
entries.example_academic: The reported cases are only the tip of the iceberg.
entries.example_spoken: Those two complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.

entries.definition: at the beginning again, because an earlier attempt failed
entries.example_academic: When the second trial failed, the researchers were back to square one.
entries.example_spoken: The file got deleted, so we're back to square one.

entries.definition: to do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often lowering the quality
entries.example_academic: Contractors who cut corners on materials were later held responsible for the collapse.
entries.example_spoken: Don't cut corners on the references; she checks them.

entries.definition: to make more effort than is expected in order to achieve something
entries.translation_fr: faire un effort supplémentaire, en faire plus
entries.example_academic: Firms that go the extra mile for their customers tend to keep them.
entries.example_spoken: She really went the extra mile to help me with my application.

entries.definition: a practical and approximate way of doing or measuring something, based on experience
entries.example_academic: As a rule of thumb, a sample should be at least ten times the number of variables.
entries.example_spoken: My rule of thumb is two hours of study for every hour of class.

entries.definition: to learn how to do something, especially when it is not simple at first
entries.translation_fr: prendre le coup de main pour
entries.example_academic: New users generally get the hang of the software within a week.
entries.example_spoken: It took me a month to get the hang of the citation style.

entries.definition: a situation in which someone has to learn a lot in a short time
entries.example_academic: New recruits face a steep learning curve in their first six months.
entries.example_spoken: There's a steep learning curve in that class, but it gets easier.

entries.definition: to decide how to act as a situation develops instead of planning ahead
entries.example_academic: With no reliable forecast, the organizers had to play it by ear.
entries.example_spoken: I don't know when I'll finish; let's play it by ear.

entries.definition: the final problem in a series that makes a situation impossible to accept
entries.translation_fr: la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase
entries.example_academic: The new tax was the last straw for merchants already burdened by tolls.
entries.example_spoken: The broken heater was the last straw; I'm moving out.

entries.definition: suddenly and unexpectedly
entries.example_academic: The announcement came out of the blue and surprised even senior officials.
entries.example_spoken: She called me out of the blue after two years.

entries.definition: to avoid talking about something unpleasant, or to say as little as possible about it
entries.example_academic: The official history glosses over the famine that followed the reform.
entries.example_spoken: He glossed over the fact that we're already a week late.

entries.definition: to depend completely on something
entries.example_academic: The success of the scheme hinges on the cooperation of local farmers.
entries.example_spoken: Everything hinges on whether we get the room.

entries.definition: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem
entries.translation_fr: se débattre avec, être aux prises avec
entries.example_academic: Economists are still grappling with the causes of the slowdown.
entries.example_spoken: I've been grappling with this proof all week.

entries.definition: to develop or end in a particular way, especially successfully
entries.example_academic: Few of the early predictions about the technology panned out.
entries.example_spoken: The internship didn't pan out, so I'm looking again.

entries.definition: to think carefully about something for a long time before deciding
entries.example_academic: The board mulled over the proposal for several months before rejecting it.
entries.example_spoken: Give me the weekend to mull it over.

entries.definition: to avoid doing something because you are nervous or not confident
entries.example_academic: Earlier studies shied away from questions of responsibility.
entries.example_spoken: Don't shy away from asking questions in the seminar.

entries.definition: to keep something bad from happening for a time
entries.example_academic: Emergency loans staved off the collapse of the banking system.
entries.example_spoken: I ate a banana to stave off hunger until dinner.

entries.definition: something that has both good and bad effects
entries.example_academic: Cheap credit proved a double-edged sword for small farmers.
entries.example_spoken: Working from home is a double-edged sword: more freedom, less focus.

entries.definition: to argue about very small and unimportant differences
entries.translation_fr: couper les cheveux en quatre, chipoter
entries.example_academic: The reviewers accused the author of splitting hairs over terminology.
entries.example_spoken: Let's not split hairs; the two versions say the same thing.

entries.definition: very different from something
entries.example_academic: The final agreement was a far cry from the ambitious plan first proposed.
entries.example_spoken: This dorm is a far cry from my room at home.

entries.definition: an obvious problem that people avoid discussing
entries.translation_fr: le sujet tabou, le problème que tout le monde évite
entries.example_academic: Funding was the elephant in the room throughout the conference.
entries.example_spoken: Nobody mentioned the elephant in the room: half the team hadn't done anything.

entries.definition: what you would expect to happen, especially when it is not good
entries.example_academic: Delays of this kind are par for the course in large public projects.
entries.example_spoken: The printer's broken again, which is par for the course.

entries.definition: a request or task that is very difficult to carry out
entries.example_academic: Halving emissions within a decade is a tall order for any economy.
entries.example_spoken: Finishing by Monday is a tall order, but we'll try.

entries.definition: to protect yourself against something harmful or unpleasant
entries.example_academic: Vitamin C is often taken to ward off colds.
entries.example_spoken: I drink a lot of tea to ward off the cold.
entries.example_interview: I keep a strict sleep schedule to ward off stress during exam season.
entries.example_discussion: Regular checkups help ward off serious illness, which is why I support Lena's plan.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Protecting in advance, often against illness, danger or criticism. Close to "stave off" (delay).

entries.definition: to try hard to get support, interest or business
entries.example_academic: The candidates toured the region to drum up support.
entries.example_spoken: We're trying to drum up interest in the club.
entries.example_interview: We put posters everywhere to drum up interest in our charity concert.
entries.example_discussion: Free food is the easiest way to drum up attendance at campus events, I think.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Almost always with "support", "interest" or "business". Separable but usually unseparated.

entries.definition: to start an event, a discussion or an activity
entries.example_academic: The conference kicked off with a keynote on climate.
entries.example_spoken: Let's kick off with introductions.
entries.example_interview: I usually kick off my day with a short run before classes.
entries.example_discussion: To kick off the discussion, I'd say the main issue is cost, not quality.
entries.usage_note: Informal. From football. Useful to open a spoken answer: "To kick things off, …". Noun: "the kickoff".

entries.definition: to find and remove something bad completely
entries.example_academic: The new director promised to root out corruption.
entries.example_spoken: We need to root out the bugs before launch.
entries.example_interview: In my internship, my task was to root out errors in old customer records.
entries.example_discussion: Stricter checks could root out plagiarism, but they should not punish honest mistakes.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Strong: removing completely after searching. Close to "weed out" (removing weaker members of a group).

entries.definition: to disapprove of something
entries.example_academic: Many universities frown on unpaid internships.
entries.example_spoken: My parents frown on video games.
entries.example_interview: In my family, being late for dinner is frowned on.
entries.example_discussion: Copying from websites is rightly frowned on, but quoting with citations is fine.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often passive: "is frowned on/upon". "Upon" is more formal than "on".

entries.definition: to start working seriously and with effort
entries.example_academic: Students who buckle down early rarely panic before exams.
entries.example_spoken: I really need to buckle down this week.
entries.example_interview: After failing a quiz, I buckled down and studied every evening.
entries.example_discussion: Clear deadlines help students buckle down, which supports Daniel's proposal.
entries.usage_note: Informal. About committing to hard work. Close to "knuckle down".

entries.definition: to continue doing something until it is finished, despite difficulties
entries.translation_fr: mener à terme, aller jusqu'au bout de
entries.example_academic: The mayor vowed to see the reforms through.
entries.example_spoken: Once I start a project, I see it through.
collocations: see it through to the end
entries.example_interview: I wanted to quit my first job, but I decided to see the contract through.
entries.example_discussion: Funding a program for one year is useless; the city must see it through.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Separable: "see sth through". Different from "see through sb" (understand their real intentions).

entries.definition: to introduce something gradually, in stages
entries.example_academic: The new tax will be phased in over three years.
entries.example_spoken: They're phasing in the new app slowly.
entries.example_interview: My school phased in laptops one grade at a time.
entries.example_discussion: Rather than an immediate ban, the university could phase in the rule over a year.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often passive: "be phased in over". Opposite: "phase out".

entries.definition: to prepare for an event or activity
entries.example_academic: Retailers are gearing up for the holiday season.
entries.example_spoken: We're gearing up for finals.
entries.example_interview: I'm currently gearing up for my final exams, so I study every evening.
entries.example_discussion: Since students are gearing up for exams in May, events should happen earlier.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Usually in continuous forms: "We're gearing up for…".

entries.definition: to delay doing something
entries.example_academic: The board decided to hold off on any new hiring.
entries.example_spoken: Hold off on buying the book until class starts.
entries.example_interview: I held off on buying a car until I knew where I would work.
entries.example_discussion: The college should hold off on the new building until enrollment figures are clear.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Followed by a noun or -ing. Irregular: held. Softer than "cancel".

entries.definition: to find something by chance
entries.example_academic: Researchers stumbled upon the effect while testing another drug.
entries.example_spoken: I stumbled upon a great café yesterday.
entries.example_interview: I stumbled upon my favorite podcast while looking for something else.
entries.example_discussion: Many discoveries are stumbled upon, so research funding should allow some freedom.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "stumble on/across". Suggests luck. Close to "come across".

entries.definition: to decide that someone or something is a failure or not worth attention
entries.translation_fr: faire une croix sur, considérer comme perdu
entries.example_academic: Critics wrote off the film before its release.
entries.example_spoken: Don't write me off yet.
entries.example_interview: My teachers almost wrote me off in tenth grade, but I proved them wrong.
entries.example_discussion: We should not write off older students as unable to learn new technology.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also financial: "write off a debt" (cancel it). Irregular: wrote, written.

entries.definition: to use something for support when other things fail
entries.example_academic: When funding ran out, the team fell back on volunteers.
entries.example_spoken: If I don't get the job, I can fall back on my savings.
entries.example_interview: I learned to cook so I would have a skill to fall back on.
entries.example_discussion: Students without family support have nothing to fall back on, as Kim points out.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Something to fall back on" is a common phrase. Irregular: fell, fallen.

entries.definition: to prepare and write a document such as a plan, list or contract
entries.example_academic: The committee drew up a list of recommendations.
entries.example_spoken: We drew up a schedule for the trip.
entries.example_interview: Before moving, I drew up a budget to see what I could afford.
entries.example_discussion: The college should draw up clear rules on AI use before the next semester.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. For formal documents. Irregular: drew, drawn. Not "draw" a picture.

entries.definition: to finish something you have started or promised
entries.translation_fr: aller jusqu'au bout, tenir ses engagements
entries.example_academic: Few governments follow through on climate pledges.
entries.example_spoken: You said you'd help, so follow through.
entries.example_interview: I promised myself I would run a marathon, and I followed through.
entries.example_discussion: Announcing a plan is easy; the problem is that schools rarely follow through on it.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Follow through on/with sth". Noun: "follow-through". Valued trait in job interviews.

entries.definition: to give money or help, along with others; or to add a comment
entries.example_academic: Residents chipped in to repair the playground.
entries.example_spoken: We all chipped in for her gift.
entries.example_interview: My roommates and I chip in every week for groceries.
entries.example_discussion: If every student chipped in five dollars, the club could afford a speaker.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Two senses: contributing money and adding a comment ("Can I chip in here?").

entries.definition: to start dealing with a problem in a much stricter way
entries.example_academic: The city is cracking down on illegal parking.
entries.example_spoken: My school cracked down on phones in class.
entries.example_interview: My high school cracked down on lateness, and it actually worked.
entries.example_discussion: Cracking down on cheating is necessary, but better exam design would help more.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Noun: "a crackdown on". Common in news about crime, cheating or fraud.

entries.definition: to think or talk too much about something, especially something bad
entries.example_academic: The report does not dwell on past failures.
entries.example_spoken: Don't dwell on it; everyone makes mistakes.
entries.example_interview: I try not to dwell on bad grades; I look at what I can improve.
entries.example_discussion: Rather than dwell on past mistakes, the council should focus on next year's budget.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often negative advice: "don't dwell on it". Irregular: dwelt (or dwelled).

entries.definition: to explain or present something clearly and in detail
entries.example_academic: The author lays out three arguments against the policy.
entries.example_spoken: Let me lay out the options.
entries.example_interview: In my interview, I laid out my plan for the first year step by step.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah lays out the costs clearly, but he ignores the long-term benefits.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Precise verb for presenting ideas or plans. Irregular: laid. Noun "layout" = arrangement.

entries.definition: to reduce the size or amount of something
entries.example_academic: The company scaled back its expansion plans.
entries.example_spoken: I had to scale back my hours at work.
entries.example_interview: I scaled back my social life during my final year to focus on my thesis.
entries.example_discussion: Scaling back the festival would save money without canceling it entirely.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Common with plans, budgets, ambitions. Also "scale down".

entries.definition: to be fully understood or realized, often slowly
entries.translation_fr: être pleinement compris, faire son chemin
entries.example_academic: The scale of the disaster took weeks to sink in.
entries.example_spoken: It still hasn't sunk in that I passed.
entries.example_interview: When I got my acceptance letter, it took days for the news to sink in.
entries.example_discussion: The cost of the plan only sinks in when you look at it per student.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Subject is the news or idea. Irregular: sank, sunk.

entries.definition: to explain something very clearly and in detail
entries.example_academic: The contract spells out the rights of each party.
entries.example_spoken: Do I have to spell it out for you?
entries.example_interview: My manager spelled out exactly what she expected in my first week.
entries.example_discussion: The syllabus should spell out the penalties for late work, as Mia suggests.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Spell it out" can sound impatient in conversation. Spelled/spelt.

entries.definition: to mention a subject briefly
entries.example_academic: The lecture only touched on the economic causes.
entries.example_spoken: We touched on that in class.
entries.example_interview: In my essay, I only touched on my family, because the topic was my work.
entries.example_discussion: Lena touches on cost, but the bigger issue she raises is fairness.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Brief mention, unlike "deal with" or "discuss". Also "touch upon" (more formal).

entries.definition: to relax after work; or to bring an activity gradually to an end
entries.example_academic: The company is winding down its operations in Asia.
entries.example_spoken: I read before bed to wind down.
entries.example_interview: To wind down after classes, I usually go for a walk.
entries.example_discussion: The research center is winding down, so students need to know where projects will move.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Pronounced /waɪnd/ like "kind". Irregular: wound /waʊnd/.

entries.definition: to finish an activity, meeting or task
entries.example_academic: The talks wrapped up without an agreement.
entries.example_spoken: Let's wrap up and go home.
entries.example_interview: To wrap up, I would say this job fits both my skills and my goals.
entries.example_discussion: Before we wrap up this thread, I want to add a point about costs.
entries.usage_note: Informal. "To wrap up, …" is a natural closing signal in a spoken answer. Also "wrap up warm" (clothes).

entries.definition: to be missed or forgotten by a system that should deal with it
entries.translation_fr: passer entre les mailles du filet
entries.example_academic: Without a tracking system, vulnerable students fall through the cracks.
entries.example_spoken: My application fell through the cracks somehow.
collocations: let sb fall through the cracks
entries.example_interview: In my first year, my scholarship form fell through the cracks, so I learned to follow up.
entries.example_discussion: Part-time students often fall through the cracks, which is why Mia wants an advisor for them.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "slip through the cracks". Typical in Listening about advising offices and paperwork.

entries.headword: bite off more than you can chew
entries.definition: to try to do more than you are able to manage
entries.translation_fr: avoir les yeux plus gros que le ventre
entries.example_academic: The guide warns new teaching assistants: do not bite off more than you can chew in your first term.
entries.example_spoken: Don't bite off more than you can chew this semester.
collocations: bite off more than one can chew
entries.ipa: /baɪt ɒf mɔːr ðæn juː kæn tʃuː/
entries.example_interview: In my first job, I learned the hard way that you should never bite off more than you can chew.
entries.example_discussion: Five clubs and a job? As the saying goes, never bite off more than you can chew.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Pronoun changes: "more than I/they can chew". Common advice in campus conversations.

entries.definition: to start studying hard
entries.example_academic: Most students hit the books only in the last week of term.
entries.example_spoken: I need to hit the books tonight.
entries.example_interview: During finals week, I hit the books from eight in the morning until dinner.
entries.example_discussion: Students hit the books harder when exams are spaced out, so Daniel's schedule makes sense.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Very common in student conversations. Past: hit (unchanged).

entries.definition: to learn how to do a job or how a system works
entries.example_academic: New interns spend the first month learning the ropes.
entries.example_spoken: I'm still learning the ropes at the lab.
entries.example_interview: At my first job, an older colleague helped me learn the ropes.
entries.example_discussion: Peer mentors help first-year students learn the ropes faster than any website.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Also "show sb the ropes" and "know the ropes". From sailing.

entries.definition: a short course that teaches a lot in a very short time
entries.example_academic: The hospital offers nurses a crash course in emergency care.
entries.example_spoken: I took a crash course in Excel last week.
entries.example_interview: Before moving to Spain, I took a two-week crash course in Spanish.
entries.example_discussion: A crash course in budgeting during orientation would help students more than another lecture.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "A crash course in sth". Also figurative: "a crash course in adult life".

entries.definition: to work or study late into the night
entries.example_academic: Researchers burned the midnight oil to meet the grant deadline.
entries.example_spoken: I've been burning the midnight oil all week.
entries.example_interview: Before my thesis deadline, I burned the midnight oil for two weeks.
entries.example_discussion: If students regularly burn the midnight oil, the workload is the problem, not their discipline.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Less extreme than "pull an all-nighter" (no sleep at all).

entries.definition: to start an activity or process
entries.example_academic: The grant helped get the ball rolling on the new research center.
entries.example_spoken: Let's get the ball rolling on the project.
entries.example_interview: To get the ball rolling on my job search, I updated my profile first.
entries.example_discussion: A small pilot program would get the ball rolling without a huge budget.
entries.usage_note: Informal. "On sth". Useful in Listening when students plan a project.

entries.definition: to make contact with someone briefly to exchange news or check progress
entries.example_academic: The advisor touches base with each student once a month.
entries.example_spoken: Let's touch base after the meeting.
entries.example_interview: I touch base with my thesis supervisor every Friday.
entries.example_discussion: Advisors should touch base with first-year students early, before problems grow.
entries.usage_note: Informal, very common in offices and campus. "Touch base with sb". Never "touch the base".

entries.definition: later than planned
entries.example_academic: Construction of the library is two months behind schedule.
entries.example_spoken: We're a bit behind schedule on our project.
entries.example_interview: My group project fell behind schedule because one member was sick.
entries.example_discussion: Since most projects run behind schedule, the deadline should include a margin.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Opposite: "ahead of schedule"; "on schedule" = on time. Not "in retard".

entries.definition: more advanced or modern than others
entries.translation_fr: en avance sur son temps, à la pointe
entries.example_academic: The college was ahead of the curve in offering online degrees.
entries.example_spoken: She's always ahead of the curve with tech.
entries.example_interview: I took a coding class early to stay ahead of the curve in my field.
entries.example_discussion: Universities that teach AI skills now will be ahead of the curve in five years.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Opposite: "behind the curve". Common in business and tech talk.

entries.definition: something that has little chance of success
entries.translation_fr: pari risqué, coup tenté sans grand espoir
entries.example_academic: Winning the grant was a long shot, but the team applied anyway.
entries.example_spoken: It's a long shot, but I'll ask.
entries.example_interview: Applying to that program was a long shot, but I got in.
entries.example_discussion: Getting the city to pay for it is a long shot, so we need a backup plan.
entries.usage_note: Informal. "It's a long shot, but…" introduces a hopeful attempt. "Not by a long shot" = not at all.

entries.headword: the ball is in your court
entries.definition: it is now your turn to act or decide
entries.translation_fr: la balle est dans votre camp
entries.example_academic: After the offer, the ball is in your court.
entries.example_spoken: I sent my answer, so the ball is in your court now.
collocations: the ball is in their court
entries.example_interview: My coach told me: I have given you the plan, so the ball is in your court.
entries.example_discussion: Professor, the survey results are clear, so I would say the ball is in your court now.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Pronoun changes: "in their/his court". Same image as in French.

entries.definition: to start a new activity with energy and immediate success
entries.example_academic: New staff are expected to hit the ground running.
entries.example_spoken: I want to hit the ground running at my new job.
collocations: be ready to hit the ground running
synonyms: get off to a flying start
entries.example_interview: I read the course materials in summer so I could hit the ground running in September.
entries.example_discussion: Summer bridge programs help students hit the ground running in their first semester.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Very common in job interviews and job ads.

entries.definition: something that makes you think seriously
entries.example_academic: The findings offer food for thought for policymakers.
entries.example_spoken: That lecture gave me a lot of food for thought.
entries.example_interview: A conversation with a nurse gave me food for thought about my career choice.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah's figures give us food for thought, even if I do not share his conclusion.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Polite way to acknowledge a classmate's idea in a discussion.

entries.definition: to make a mistake by failing to do something you were responsible for
entries.translation_fr: ne pas assurer, commettre une négligence
entries.example_academic: The agency dropped the ball on flood warnings.
entries.example_spoken: Sorry, I dropped the ball on that email.
entries.example_interview: I once dropped the ball on a group deadline, and I learned to use a planner.
entries.example_discussion: The university dropped the ball by not telling students about the fee change earlier.
entries.usage_note: Informal. "Drop the ball on sth". Admitting it ("I dropped the ball") sounds honest and natural.

entries.definition: used to say that a plan has failed and you must start again
entries.translation_fr: retour à la case départ (pour repenser le projet)
entries.example_academic: When the prototype failed, engineers went back to the drawing board.
entries.example_spoken: The client hated it, so it's back to the drawing board.
collocations: go back to the drawing board
entries.example_interview: My first business plan was rejected, so it was back to the drawing board.
entries.example_discussion: If the survey shows no demand, it is back to the drawing board for the app.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Focus on redesigning, unlike "back to square one" (losing all progress).

entries.definition: to do many difficult or unnecessary things to get something
entries.translation_fr: faire des pieds et des mains, passer par mille formalités
entries.example_academic: Applicants must jump through hoops to get a visa.
entries.example_spoken: I had to jump through hoops to change my major.
synonyms: go through a lot of red tape
entries.example_interview: I had to jump through hoops to get my credits transferred from my old school.
entries.example_discussion: Students should not have to jump through hoops just to get a refund.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Often critical of bureaucracy. "Make sb jump through hoops".

entries.definition: a situation in which you either succeed by your own efforts or fail
entries.example_academic: Many interns are left to sink or swim.
entries.example_spoken: At my first job, it was sink or swim.
collocations: leave sb to sink or swim
entries.example_interview: My first week abroad was sink or swim, and it made me more confident.
entries.example_discussion: Leaving new students to sink or swim is unfair, so I support the mentoring plan.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Often critical: "leave sb to sink or swim".

entries.definition: to become nervous and decide not to do something you planned
entries.example_academic: Investors got cold feet after the first losses.
entries.example_spoken: I almost got cold feet before my presentation.
entries.example_interview: I nearly got cold feet before moving abroad, but my friends encouraged me.
entries.example_discussion: Many students get cold feet about studying abroad because of costs, not fear.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Also used about weddings. "Get cold feet about sth".

entries.definition: following the rules exactly
entries.translation_fr: dans les règles, selon le règlement
entries.example_academic: The audit found that the lab had done everything by the book.
entries.example_spoken: My boss does everything by the book.
entries.example_interview: As a lab assistant, I learned to do everything by the book.
entries.example_discussion: Doing things by the book is safer, but it can make the process very slow.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Can be positive (honest) or negative (rigid). Opposite: "cut corners".

entries.definition: to share ideas with someone to get their opinion
entries.translation_fr: tester des idées auprès de quelqu'un
entries.example_academic: Researchers often bounce ideas off colleagues before writing a proposal.
entries.example_spoken: Can I bounce some ideas off you?
entries.example_interview: I like to bounce ideas off my roommate before I start an essay.
entries.example_discussion: Study rooms give students a place to bounce ideas off each other.
entries.usage_note: Informal. "Bounce ideas off sb". Close to "run sth by sb".

entries.definition: a difficult decision
entries.example_academic: Choosing between the two candidates was a tough call for the committee.
entries.example_spoken: It's a tough call, but I'd pick the first one.
entries.example_interview: Last spring I had two job offers, and picking one was a really tough call.
entries.example_discussion: It is a tough call, but I would fund the library before the gym.
entries.usage_note: Informal. "It's a tough call, but…" is a natural way to start an opinion.

entries.definition: to be good enough to be chosen or to succeed
entries.example_academic: Only a third of the applicants made the cut.
entries.example_spoken: I didn't make the cut for the team.
entries.example_interview: I tried out for the varsity team, but I did not make the cut.
entries.example_discussion: If only top students make the cut, the program will not reach those who need it.
entries.usage_note: Informal. From sports (golf, team selection). Often negative: "didn't make the cut".

entries.definition: to wait until the next day before deciding
entries.translation_fr: la nuit porte conseil, y réfléchir jusqu'au lendemain
entries.example_academic: Negotiators agreed to sleep on it and meet again.
entries.example_spoken: Let me sleep on it and I'll tell you tomorrow.
entries.example_interview: When I got the job offer, I asked to sleep on it before accepting.
entries.example_discussion: For a decision this big, the council should sleep on it rather than vote tonight.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Polite way to delay a decision. Irregular: slept.

entries.definition: something that seems bad at first but has good results
entries.example_academic: Losing the contract proved a blessing in disguise for the firm.
entries.example_spoken: Failing that class was a blessing in disguise.
collocations: turn out to be a blessing in disguise
entries.example_interview: Losing my first job was a blessing in disguise, because it led me to this field.
entries.example_discussion: The budget cut may be a blessing in disguise if it forces the club to find sponsors.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Usually "turn out to be / prove a blessing in disguise".
